name: Abena Osei-Grant
languages: Enough Spanish, Mandarin and Haitian Creole to triage in
equipment: Medkit (her own go-bag: gauze, tourniquets, chest seals, saline, suture kit, gloves, a penlight and a stethoscope)
Trauma shears in a scrub-pocket holster
Painkillers (ibuprofen and acetaminophen, about 40 doses) and one blister pack of something stronger she should not have taken home
Mercy Eastgate Hospital staff ID and a badge reel
Scrubs under a down coat, and clogs she regrets
Water bottle, two granola bars and a banana going brown
Phone (34% battery) with a lock-screen photo of two boys in matching football kits
features: Human (+1 to all six ability scores)
Field Medicine (action: with a medkit, heal 1d6+4 hit points (1d6 + WIS 3 + level 1), or stabilize a creature at 0 HP as a bonus action; 4 uses per long rest)
Triage (bonus action: Medicine check vs. DC 10 tells her the exact hit points and conditions of one creature)
Hospital Privileges (Medical Professional feature: staff at any Merriwick hospital or clinic will let her in, talk to her straight and let her use what is on the shelves)

personality.traits: I sort people. I cannot walk into a room without knowing who is going to die first, and I have learned to be kind out loud while I do it. I am very calm and it is entirely a professional skill.
personality.ideals: Treat who is in front of you. The ones you cannot reach are not your fault, and the one in front of you is your job.
personality.bonds: My boys, Kofi and Sam, eleven and nine, who are on the mainland at their father's this week, safe, thank God, on the other side of the water. And Unit 4 at Mercy Eastgate: nine patients on ventilators who cannot walk anywhere, and the night shift who will not leave them.
personality.flaws: I do not stop. I will triage a stranger while my own leg is bleeding, and I will go back into a building I should not go back into because someone in it is breathing. I am also, privately, furious all the time, and it leaks.

appearance: A tall Ghanaian-American woman of thirty-eight with close-cropped natural hair, a long neck and the stillness of someone who has stood very still beside a lot of beds. Navy scrubs under an enormous down coat, clogs, a badge reel, and a stethoscope she forgot to take off. Her hands are always clean, and she notices when yours are not.
backstory: Abena Osei-Grant has been an emergency nurse for fourteen years and the charge nurse on evenings at Mercy Eastgate for four, which means she has run the hardest room on the island through two blackouts, a crane collapse and the night the Kingsgate express derailed. She is good at it in the way people are good at things they have stopped thinking of as hard. On the Thursday she has come off a double and is in the Union Terminal concourse buying her boys birthday cards — they are with their father across the bay in Calder Point for the week, which she will later think of as the luckiest thing that has ever happened to her — when the light changes. Her first clear thought, before the screaming starts, is a count: four hundred people, one stampede, perhaps forty injuries, a dozen serious, the nearest trauma bay a mile and a half east. Her second is that the hospital will be full by six and she is not there.
